# Collinder 423: A Quiet Gathering in Cepheus

*An open cluster nearly 6,500 light-years away rewards patient searching—and a wide enough view to let its stars gather into one scene.*

Some deep-sky objects announce themselves with a bright core or a dramatic shape. Collinder 423 is subtler: a loose gathering of stars whose appeal lies in noticing the pattern emerge from the darkness. Catalogued as the open cluster NGC 6939, it sits in the northern sky at coordinates 20h 31m 40s, +60° 39′ (J2000), according to the SIMBAD astronomical database.

An open cluster is a group of stars born from the same cloud of gas and dust. Its members travel through the galaxy together, though a cluster’s gravitational hold can gradually loosen over time. Collinder 423’s measured parallax—the tiny apparent shift caused by Earth’s orbit—places it at roughly 2,000 parsecs, or about 6,500 light-years, from us. That estimate comes from inverting SIMBAD’s listed parallax of 0.506 milliarcseconds; it is a useful scale, not a claim that the cluster is a precise cosmic milepost.

The catalog gives the cluster an apparent diameter of about 14.8 arcminutes. That is roughly half the apparent width of the full Moon, though the comparison describes the cluster’s span on the sky, not a glowing disk with a sharp edge. The stars are individual points of light, and how many stand out depends on your instrument, the sky, and your eyes.

There is a pleasing change of scale in the view. At the eyepiece, the cluster is a small patch of stars against a much larger field. In your imagination, each point is a sun at a distance thousands of light-years beyond the nearby stars that share the same view. The database also lists a radial velocity of about −18.6 kilometres per second: measured along our line of sight, the cluster’s average motion is toward us. It is a reminder that a star field is not still, even when it appears fixed.

**How to find it:** Enter the coordinates above into a planetarium app or telescope GoTo system, checking that the app is using the J2000 position. Collinder 423’s high northern declination makes it a practical target for many northern observers, but its altitude and best viewing time depend on your location and the season. Give your eyes time to adapt to darkness, choose a moonless night if possible, and begin with a low-power eyepiece. The listed 14.8-arcminute extent suggests a field wide enough to hold the cluster comfortably, with some surrounding sky for context. If the stars seem sparse at first, pause and look slightly away from the center; averted vision can help faint points become more apparent.

A small telescope is a good place to start, while binoculars may show the brighter members under a dark sky. Avoid rushing to high magnification: the goal is not to enlarge each star, but to see how the points relate as a group. Collinder 423 offers no grand explosion or bright cloud—just a quiet assembly, far away and still moving, waiting for the sky to settle around it.

**Source:** [SIMBAD: NGC 6939](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%206939) (object classification, coordinates, parallax, radial velocity, and angular size).
